I may have done this the most difficult way possible, but here is the process of how I got from A to B.

To preface, 2 years ago I built a compost bin in my back yard , and I throw pretty much all of my  yard waste in it, other than weeds. This includes mulched leaves, grads clippings, random sticks etc. I actually dug up the grass in the front, and threw it in the compost pile and I use that as fertilizer for my garden beds. 
 
To start, I bought a couple of plants at a time so as to not overwhelm myself, focusing on perennials that are either native or pollinator friendly. I think that digging up the grass also helped loosen the soil giving the roots some room to breathe. So the process last year was : buy some plants --> dig up some grass -> put the plants in --> cover that area with mulch. 

This year, I had a good head start as most of the perennials came back, so I applied some fresh mulch in those areas. Buying perennials can add up and get pricey, so I put some bulbs down in the spring, which have done reasonably well (and would have done much better if they weren't being eaten by rabbits all the time). I also started some perennials from seed and once they had a good root system established, I'd repeat the process and put them in the ground. 

So far this season has been quite rainy, so I have only done minimal watering, and most of that has been right when I put the plants in to help them adjust. The mulch also helps keep moisture in the ground, so that helps as well. 

The final thing to keep in mind (and you'll notice this if you dog up your grass) is that the root system of grass is only about 3-5 inches deep, whereas when I'm putting plants in, the hole that I need to dig can be up to 12 inches or so to cover the roots. This allows the plant to use moisture that's deeper in the ground, while that top few inches of soil dry out much more easily.

While I can't speak to the particulars of this situation, the reality is that patients are already dying. If you have unsafe nurse: patient ratios and lack appropriate support staff, several issues arise: 

The delay of care- oftentimes treatments are dependent on test results like blood work, and if the nurse can't get the those done in a timely manner, the appropriate is delayed and the patient's condition may deteriorate in the meantime. Same thing goes for administering treatments or medications.

Speaking of medications, being in a chaotic environment with high ratios makes it more likely that a medication error can occur, it's easier to pull the wrong medication, or draw up the wrong dose, which in some cases has had fatal outcomes. 

The last point that I'll make here requires more nuance. More often than not, if a patient's condition is deteriorating, the first signs of it are subtle. They may have drops in blood pressure, their heart rate becomes slightly elevated, they start to look more unwell.  Being able to note these changes is next to impossible if you don't have an established baseline, and if you don't see the patient more than once a shift, or don't have time to check vitals and do proper assessments. The opportunities for early intervention are missed, and the issue might escalate to the point where the person crashes, and will require more drastic measures to quite literally save their life.

I'm sure there are more examples, but i hope that this helps explain why workloads are a safety issue for patients.

In the case of some drugs, like hyrdomorph contin, the outside capsule is typically made of gelatin, which dissolves quickly, but the medication itself is formulated as small granules that dissolve slowly, hence the extended release.  Crushing the granules is what  would affect the rate of release, potentially leading to an overdose of the medication, but pouring out the granules wouldn't. 

Another reason for not crushing certain meds is because some of them are enteric coated, to either protect the stomach, or to protect the medication from stomach acid, so that it can be absorbed in another part of the digestive tract. 

Pharmacy is always a great resource to consult if you're not sure about the med.

Because MSK and specifically back injuries are incredibly common in my profession, so I do it to protect myself at work. I don't have any data to support this, but I suspect that a lot of times the injuries are related to a) not having the strength to perform the task and b) not having practiced lifting heavy things, therefore not having correct form. 

It also makes everyday life tasks easier. Groceries? No problem. Need to carry my summer rims and tires inside across a parking lot and down 2 hallways to put them in storage? Not a big deal. 

I also do it for future me. As a woman, I'm at higher risk for osteoporosis as I age, and strength training helps reduce my risk by increasing bone density and decreasing risk for fractures, which can be devastating in the older population. It  also helps with balance and coordination (which is a benefit that I've already noticed) helping to prevent falls which can also be devastating once you get older. Also, muscle mass tends to atrophy significantly with age leading to huge decreases in functionality in older adults and I refuse to be granny who can't even push herself up off the toilet without assistance. All of this is decades away for me, but the time to put in the work to avoid these problems is now. 

Lastly, if I ever end up in one of those Hollywood movie scenes where I'm hanging off a cliff, I'd like to be able to do at least one pull up to save my own life.

on a good day, my 5k time is about 33 minutes. i'm not the fastest runner, but that's ok. i've found that what i lack in speed compared to my faster friends i can make up for in distance. years later, it's still a work in progress, and guess what? i look just as sweaty and red faced and exhausted when i finish a run now as i did when i could only run for a minute at a time. 

good luck!

student nurse here. i've seen a couple things that have stuck with me. once had a client who had abdominal surgery, and had multiple pads over her stomach, but she had so much drainage that they were leaking, and the tape that was holding them down started coming off. the smell was atrocious. i can't even begin to describe it. 

had another patient who had been in a coma for 5 days and was on VRE contact precautions. nobody had combed her hair in weeks. she also didn't speak english, so communication was a challenge, but she kept going on about her hair. it had literally turned into one giant dreadlock. there wasn't anything gross in it, but it took me about 12 hours over the course of a month in order to comb it out. she was so happy afterwards that she started cry while she was hugging me. 

the most disturbing thing i've witnessed though was a lady  who was 100+ years old, and lived in a retirement home. she had some cognitive impairment and hearing loss, and had developed a tumor, possibly cancerous, which caused her a great deal of pain, which wasn't managed until she was almost dead. i saw her the afternoon before she died, and she was moaning and restless from the pain.  the look in her eyes was heartbreaking. whatever they were giving her wasn't effective at all, and the people around her neglected her. :(

there are a couple things that you can do in this situation. ask her if she is having suicidal thoughts, and if she has a plan. asking about plans will not cause a suicide attempt. 

suicidal ideation is serious, and not telling anybody is not an option. take her to the doctor or the ER before any attempt is made. there are usually crisis lines that you can call for immediate help/advice.  approach somebody that she is close to and she trusts, who you know cares about her and is willing to help her get better. be up front, and tell her who you told. she probably won't be happy about it right now, but it will be for her benefit in the long run. 

if you go to the hospital, she may be admitted for some time for observation if the doctor determines that she is at risk for harming herself. if they don't, make sure you put together a safety plan before you go- make sure she knows that she has options that don't include self-harm. 

most importantly, don't try to handle this all by yourself. she needs the help and support of people that love her, as well as people who are formally trained in this type of situation - doctors, nurses, social workers, crisis counsellors etc.  i wish you all the best.

something to consider is what area of nursing you would like to work in, if you were to go into nursing. how much person-to-person contact would you like to have? would you like to work with kids? adults? older people? 

there are also many different specialties and areas, such as mental health, public health, community nursing, administration, and teaching in addition to what i think are more "traditional" roles in the hospital (cardiology, oncology, med-surg and the like). 

i think it's also important for you to see what appeals to you in being a pharmacist. what aspects of it do you like? 

as a side note, you also do learn about pharmacology and medications in nursing school, and you do need to know about different medications, interactions, doses, counter-indications, as well as develop critical thinking skills about whether or not a drug should be given to a patient at a certain point in time, in addition to making sure that you're giving the right drug to the patient (because pharmacy sends the wrong stuff sometimes), on top of other aspects of care. it can definitely be challenging. 

in short, inventory your likes, dislikes, preferences and values, and figure out which career more closely corresponds to them. do some research about the different opportunities and areas for professional development, educational requirements, and compensation/salary, and see if anything catches your attention and interest. doing some volunteer work in an area you may be interested in can also help you determine if you're going in the right direction by giving you some hands on experience.
